utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. It's Monday, November 2009 [as interpreted]. I'd like to greet the accused present in the courtroom, the Defence counsel, the Prosecution, the expert witness. I'd like to make a short administrative announcement to the Petkovic Defence. We have seen your schedule for the upcoming witnesses. Thank you for providing that. I'd simply like to point out that on the 10th of December -- Thursday, the 10th of December, there's a plenary of the Judges on that day, and as a result the Chamber will not be able to hold a hearing. But when I have a look at the schedule, as I note that the witness for the previous week, Mr. Filip Filipovic, is supposed to testify for four hours over six days, Peric, Bozo, the witness Peric, Bozo, could be called on the Monday, as early as Monday, so if we finish with Mr. Filipovic, we could then continue with Mr. Peric, and we could conclude with him on the 9th of December, Wednesday the 9th. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good afternoon to you and everybody in the courtroom. Thank you for your suggestion. We were, indeed, going to bring Mr. Peric earlier than we'd planned, and we wanted to prepare him to enter the courtroom one or two days before it was originally scheduled. We expect that General Filipovic will not testify for six days, as has been planned. It will all depend on the other Defence teams, whether they will need to cross-examine or not. In any case, we will respect your suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Thank you, Ms. Alaburic. I believe that there is something that Mr. Pusic would like to inform the Chamber of. Would you like to do that in open session or in private session? THE ACCUSED PUSIC: [Interpretation] In open session, Your Honour. I would like to thank the Trial Chamber and the OTP for the understanding they showed on the occasion of the death of my father. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pusic, as you know, we found out about this last week, and the Chamber does what is necessary so that you can leave immediately for Mostar to attend your father's funeral. We express our condolences. I've already informed your counsel that they should convey our condolences to you. We will now continue with the Prosecution cross-examination. So that it is in the transcript, I would like to state the following: I committed a slip of the tongue last week and I mentioned the name of Colonel Merdan, whereas, in fact, I had Colonel Siber in mind. And Mr. Praljak intervened with that respect. So the name I had in mind was Colonel Siber. Madam West, I greet you once more, and I will give you the floor you now.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gorjanc. I hope you are well. Today, I'm going to continue asking some more questions of you, and hopefully we'll finish today. I want to back up, though, and talk about some of the testimony you gave on the first day of your direct, and that would be testimony you gave on Tuesday, and I'll read part of it so we can all go back to the same place. You were asked a question about three documents, and Ms. Alaburic said: "It should be an example of acts of sabotage that were carried out." And she noted document 4D462, which was an interview with Salko Alihodzic, and she said that it described actions taken by the population and organised by the BH Army, the Dubravska Plateau in mid-July of 1993, and she asked you to look at the document. And your answer was: "I happen to be familiar with this area. I know for a fact that the area was HVO controlled at the time. There were no BH Army units around. This is not a textbook act of sabotage, in terms of penetrating behind enemy lines in order to carry out sabotage. It is my conviction that this gentleman was probably keeping a rifle at his home. Someone then simply called him up and he joined this action. But it wasn't the unit, as such, in this case that was organised to perform this." Mr. Gorjanc, my question for you -- excuse me. She then asked you whether it was consistent with All-People's Defence, and your answer was: "Yes, it is fully consistent with the most salient premises of the doctrine." Mr. Gorjanc, for you this document that Ms. Alaburic showed you last week, this evidenced that the ABiH were employing a key component about the All-People's Defence, correct, and that would be sabotage operations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The expression "sabotage" does not completely reflect the nature of that operation. That was basically an action behind the enemy lines among the deployment of the lines of the HVO troops, and this is in keeping with the doctrine of All-People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. May we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to avoid any confusion when we are talking about at the level of the former Yugoslavia and the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In connection with this latest conclusion, are we talking about a doctrine that was a Yugoslav doctrine or are we talking about something else? I can put this question in the redirect, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Exactly, I think that's a very good suggestion. We should not really continue interrupting and standing up for things that can be done later. Please, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, we're going to move on from the All-People's Defence, and now we're going to talk about the part of your report where you write about wartime armies. And in paragraph 14 of your report, you said that a wartime army is formed in a completely different way when there is no state peacetime core army, and then you write about the difficult challenges of facing a wartime army. Do you remember this part of your report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: And is it your position that the HVO was formed under these same conditions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO was formed under extremely unfavorable conditions. I said the HVO, the ABiH, and the Army of Kosovo have roughly equally unfavorable conditions for their establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Is it your opinion that the HVO was formed from scratch, for lack of a better term?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, one could say that. The HVO didn't have any basis, not in the TO of Herzegovina or Central Bosnia, as it was then called, nor in the JNA or what remained of the JNA, nor from any other army; let us say, for example, the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, in paragraph 15 you write about insufficient training. Is it your opinion that the HVO was insufficiently trained?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Most of the soldiers of the HVO -- or, rather, all the members of the former armies of the former Yugoslavia did complete basic military training during their military service in the JNA and during military exercises. I have to point out, however, that in the area of Western Herzegovina, there were very few military exercises organised by the JNA, especially in the second half of the 1980s, for well-known reasons; the lack of confidence in the Croats and a lack of large units in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, assuming that the HVO, when it began and into its first year and a half of existence, received a number of trained soldiers from Croatia, would you agree with me that at least for these soldiers -- these soldiers from the HV in Croatia, would have been very well trained and experienced?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably they were trained, because many of them had taken part in the war against the Serbs and the JNA in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: So the answer to that question is, Yes; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Now I'd like to move to paragraph 17 of your report, and here you talk about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: There has been one element, Mr. Gorjanc, that struck me. You have stated that there was a, I quote from line 9, page 33 "lack of confidence in the Croats." Does that mean that there was a view, in government circles, military defence circles of the SFRY, about any maybe separatist or otherwise unruly, rebellious tendency in Western Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, lack of confidence was not based on the conviction that there might be a rebellion or something like that. The attitude of the military leadership, which was mostly composed of Serbs, was based on some experiences from the Second World War, and this remained in their minds. In formal and legal terms, not in any document was any mention made of -- that would go against the Croats in Western Herzegovina. However, JNA units were not developed there. Military conscripts were called up -- all called to join military units in -- mostly in Dalmatia and Mostar, and a large number of military conscripts were not reachable, as many people from that area were temporarily working in Western Europe, so they were not included in military units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I thought I understood something which I will put directly to be sure whether it is true or not. Is it the case that the Serbs more or less had a tendency of considering Croats as Ustashas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Only extreme Croatian nationalists were referred to as Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A short question. We know, because there were witnesses who told us, that before the 1990s, under the regime of Marshal Tito, there were political opponents who were in prison; for example, Tudjman. According to your own knowledge, those opponents, were they put on this list purely for political reasons, that is, because they wanted a different system that would differ from the Soviet system, or for other reasons linked to a form of autonomy of the republics, or for purely ethnic reasons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is hard for me to answer that question, as I wasn't employed in the police, or in the military, or public security systems. Why those people were listed, these persons had, in public, advocated certain national ideas. In those days, as far as I know, at least, the late President Tudjman was not in favour of secession of Croatia, but he did advocate greater autonomy of Croatia within Yugoslavia. This applied also to some Slovenian leaderships, like President Vlado Kavcic, to whom a monument was unveiled recently, and there were such leaders in Bosnia and Herzegovina as well. On the other side, there were people who advocated a firm line, an autocratic, a unified Yugoslavia, and after a certain period of time they dropped out of politics, and they were black-listed too. Many were also arrested. But this was at the end of the 1940s, to be quite honest, so it is hard to say that the reason was exclusively certain nationalist tendencies or separatist tendencies. That -- it couldn't be said that those people were persecuted for such reasons under that system.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, I want to talk to you now about your paragraph 17, which talks about chain of command, and you write there that: "Before the outbreak of an armed conflict, there is no command system which could integrate individual armed groups." You write: "Command over armed groups is mostly based on personal relations and common political or terrorist activities before the armed conflict." Mr. Gorjanc, is it your position that the HVO lacked effective command and control?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the HVO at the beginning did not have an effective system -- integrated system of command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: What documents were you shown in support of that opinion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, specifically, there is a host of documents which show that the municipal presidents had greater control over brigades than zone commanders did. At least that was the case at the beginning. Also, individual commanders were forced to beg for units to be sent to the front-line, and so on. I didn't refer to those documents in my report, believing that this was common knowledge, because any armies that have been formed ad hoc, local government is stronger than the central government.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: All right. Just so that we're clear, it is your position that the HVO lacked effective command and control, but you did not cite any HVO documents in your report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just an objection on my part. The witness, in his expert report, did not analyse the HVO and the control and command system in the HVO, but he spoke about the principle of forming wartime armies. And, Judge Trechsel, I want my objection to be recorded in the transcript because my learned friend is going outside --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: This is technically not an objection, it is commentary, and you have done so a number of times now. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Alaburic, a moment, please. As my colleague has told you just now, it is a question of re-examination. You come from the civil law system, and it is true that there this is possible, but we are now in a different system. The Prosecutor presents her ideas through her questions, and then you wait quietly for your turn to re-examine. By intervening, surely you see that you're irritating the Judges, who are forced to tell you that this is a matter for re-examination. I've already told you we are not a jury, we're not farmers. We are professional judges. Therefore, we know. We don't have to be reminded every time. Every time you get up to tell us something, we have a feeling that we don't know anything. Let the Prosecutor say what she wishes to say, and then you will have your chance during the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I want my objection to go down in the transcript because one day I will not have any rights to protect my client if I did not react on time. I did not react to my learned friend's questions about the command and control in the HVO, but I do object to whether he wrote something in his report or not and whether he supported that with documents or not, and that is why I wish to point out that this report is not a report on the HVO, but it is a report about the formation of wartime armies, as such. This report can be valid in any case, be it in Chinese or Japanese, and that is why I am saying that my learned friend is not referring to the contents of the report, because the report is not an analysis of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this prompts me to ask you a question which has been at the tip of my tongue for some time. When you prepared your report, did you read the report of the expert witness of the Prosecution, regarding the subject of control and command, by Mr. Pringle? Had you read it? Did you read that report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I received that only when my report was already finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, because in paragraph 17, when you're talking about the system of command and control - I suppose it was also about control - so you did not read the report provided by the expert witness for the OTP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I think it might be time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is time. We'll take 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, before the break my question to you had been whether it was your position that the HVO lacked effective command and control, and your answer was: "Yes, the HVO at the beginning did not have an effective system, an integrated system of command and control." Sir, when you say "at the beginning," can you give me a time-frame?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not a subject of my expert report. However, as I studied a host of documents, and as I read the descriptions of many events, I can conclude that the HVO did not have effective control from the moment the conflict broke out in 1992 until the end of 1993, or maybe a month longer, spilling into 1994. However, I did not go on studying the year 1994, so I can't be sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And I understand that you say that you've seen a number of those -- and other documents that would support that notion, but we don't have those documents here. Can you remember, offhand, any of those documents?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be very difficult for me to remember any of them. I have already emphasised in my previous answer that I didn't deal with the issue of the functioning of command and control in the HVO. I just have some information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I would like to give you some different information. And for the purposes of these questions, again, I'm going to show you some documents -- some material to you, and I'd like you to assume it to be true, and then we'll talk about whether the HVO had effective command and control. The first document is P10029, and this will shortly come up on the screen for you. This is a -- some of the testimony from the Kordic case, and it's at page 26861 where Mr. Petkovic is giving testimony. And the attorney says -- he shows him a document, and the document is dated April 18th, 1993, so April of 1993. He says: "General, if I may suggest to you that the chain of command was well identified, that it did what it was supposed to do, and that it operated in the manner that you would expect a military chain of command to operate in April of 1993. Would you agree with that?" Mr. Petkovic's answer is: "Your Honours, I have always claimed that the chain of command had been put in place and that it was in working order. I continue to affirm that." Sir, assuming that is correct, Mr. Gorjanc, would you agree with me that at least in April of 1993, a chain of command for the HVO was working well?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that. It may have functioned between the Main Staff, the commands of the zones, and some brigades. However, when it came to the level of brigades, battalions, companies, platoons, individual foot-soldiers, I believe that chain of command was very weak. You have to bear in mind that in the higher positions, in the Main Staff, and in the commands of zones and brigades, you had the former active officers of the JNA or, alternatively, the reserve officers of the JNA who had undergone the JNA schools. However, at lower levels there were people without any particular military education, nor training, especially when it comes to command and control. One might say that at the operational level, the command functioned rather well, whereas at the tactical level, especially at lower tactical levels, it left a lot to be desired.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: So just to make sure I understand what you're saying, notwithstanding General Petkovic's answer that: "I have always claimed that the chain of command was has been put in place and that it was in working order," where he does not distinguish between the higher chain of command and the lower chain of command, it is your testimony that at the lower levels it was not in working order; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Let's go to August of 1993, P04131, P04131. And we can wait for the screen, and I would just say that this is from August 12th, 1993. This is an order from General Praljak. And the first part says: "The Main Staff shall be directly subordinated to the supreme commander ..." Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: So you can review this, and it goes -- it's 1 through 8, and it talks about the chain of command. Number 1 talks about the indirectly subordinated to supreme commander. Number 2 talks about the operational zones and then the professional units. Number 3 talks about logistical support, and it goes on about communications, and finally in 6 he says -- not "finally": "I prohibit any violation of this command system." And, number 8: "This order becomes effective immediately." Sir, would you agree with me that in August of 1993, General Praljak is overseeing what appears to be a very effective chain of command?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that. If that chain of command had functioned properly, then this order would certainly not have been necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: And notwithstanding this order, can you cite for me any document that would suggest the chain of command in August of 1993 was not functioning properly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to emphasise once again that I did not particularly deal with the system of command in the HVO, or in the BH Army, for that matter. Therefore, I believe that I am not qualified enough to provide some very firm statements in respect of either one or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: I'd like to look at a document coming from December of 1993. This is P07044, P07044. It's, I believe, in the first big binder, but you can also wait for the screen. This is December 6, 1993. Okay, December 6, 1993. It's an order signed by General Petkovic, and it's to all the military districts and headquarter support units of the HVO. And it says, number 1: "Send regular daily combat reports twice a day as follows:" It says: "The morning report by 0800, with the situation at 0600, evening report by 2200." Then it says on number 2: "Use a list of questions from the guide-lines for daily combat report ..." Number 3: "ZP commands shall forward this order to their immediately subordinate units ..." Number 4: "This order shall take effect ... on December 13th." And then it appears to be sent to a number of units under his signature. Sir, would you agree with me that by December of 1993, so even by your standards, we're getting towards the end of the time-frame you spoke about earlier, and that by December of 1993 would you agree that the chain of command looks like it's operating well?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I could say no to that. One of the elements of command is also reporting, and if people needed a warning about the need to report back, that means that the chain of command is not functioning. I can say that the wording of this order is identical to the wording that could be heard in the JNA. All officers knew that they had to report back with the situation as at 1800 hours. Those were regular daily reports. And morning reports were sent with the situation as at 6.00 in the morning. Everybody had -- knew that they had to send reports. I assume that they did. But obviously they needed an additional order to that effect, which was issued in December of that year, which corroborates my claims.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: I think it might be a good idea to actually look at a string, a string of orders, and then we can ask some questions as to whether you think it was effective. And this string comes from January of 1993, so almost a year before this December document we just looked at. The first will be P01146, and this is a document January 15th, 1993, P01146. And this is a decision, and it will give you some background as to this set of orders. It's signed by Dr. Prlic. It's a decision, and this would be subsequent to the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. Sir, are you familiar with the Vance-Owen Peace Plan?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So 15 of January, number 1: "All units of the ABiH which at this moment are stationed in provinces 3, 8, and 10, which have been declared Croatian provinces in the Geneva Accords, shall be subordinated to the Command of the Main Staff of the HVO ...:" "2. All units of the HVO armed forces which at this moment are stationed in provinces 1, 5, and 9, which have been declared Muslim provinces in the Geneva Accords, shall be subordinated to the Command of the Main Staff of the ABiH." And number 3 talks about other groups and provinces that are not at issue here. Number 4 says this should be temporary, but then number 5 says: "The deadline for implementing this decision is hereby set at five days, starting from today." So this is the first order I want you to take a look at. And the next one is P01140. And you'll note on 1146, if they haven't changed it yet, there's a number on top of the date, you'll see that there's a number there. So if we go to P01140, which is dated 15 January, which is the same date, we'll see that this is an order from Bruno Stojic, and in it, in number 1, it says: "The Main Staff of the Armed Forces of the HVO shall immediately establish direct contact with all operations zones and commands of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the territories of provinces 3, 8, and 10, and 1, 5 and 9, and in order to make the decision of the HVO HZ-HB number --" and then it gives a number, "number 01-I-32/93 of the 15 January 1993 specific reports implementation." And I just -- on this order I want you to note that the number I just read out is the same number on top of the Prlic decision. It indicates towards the bottom, number 7: "The dead-line for implementing this order is 1900 hours on 20 January 1993." Now, if we can go to the next document, P01139, again it's the same date, 15 of January, and this is an order from General Petkovic. It says, on the top of it: "Pursuant to the decision of the HZ-HB HVO number ...," and it lists the same number, 01-1-32/93, that is listed on the Prlic decision, and then it says: " ... and the order of the chief of Defence Department number," and it gives "02-1/1-9," which is the same number on the Stojic order, "15 January 1993, and pursuant to the Geneva agreement on the structure of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as the jurisdiction of the Armed Forces Command in provinces, I order --" And then you'll read the order. And number 1, by now you're familiar with this. It says that: "All units of the HVO ... in 3, 8, and 10, should be placed under the HVO. And number 2 is: "All HVO units in 1, 5, and 9 ... shall be placed under the ABiH." And then number 4 says: "Members and units of the HVO armed forces and that the BH Army, who do not submit to the commands in 1 and 2 --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Dear Ms. West, please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I promise to try.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Number 4: "Members and units of the HVO Armed Forces and of the BH Army, who do not submit to the commands in items 1 and 2 herein, leave the province where they do not belong, and otherwise they will be treated as paramilitary units and disarmed." Now I'd like to go to P01135. This is dated 15 January as well. This is signed by Petkovic. It's entitled "Full combat readiness of all HVO units," and it's an order. And it says: "Due to the open treacherous aggression by Muslim forces throughout the HZ-HB territory, which has already resulted in tens of deaths and a large number of injuries among HVO members and which includes the burning of Croatian houses and the expulsion of the Croatian population, and with the aim of self-defence of the people and the territory of the HZ-HB, I hereby issue the following:" The first thing he says is: "Raise the combat readiness of the HVO units ..." And what follows are a number of items that all go to this expectation of fighting. And finally, at least in 14 -- he gives a number of details, but in 14 he says: "Regular reports shall be submitted to me for the situation as of 7.00, 12.00, 1900 and 24 hours, and interim reports shall be submitted immediately." I'll just stop here for a moment, sir. When you were talking about reports earlier, reportings, is this what you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: And so we'll move on to P01186. This is an ABiH document, so it's -- I'll note for you at the start it's not within the chain -- the same chain of command of the HVO, but it's in response to the HVO's orders, and it's signed by Pasalic, 18 January: "I have thoroughly analysed and understood your order," and then it gives a reference number, which is 01-70-93, and for the purposes of this just know that that is the same reference number on the Petkovic order of 15 January, and then he tells him -- he gives him some background information, but then he says, under number 5: "I cannot carry out item 2 of your order due to the fact that the 4th Corps of the Bosnian Army and its units are not under your command regarding such decisions and their execution." And then I'm going to look at another document, which is P01163. Again I'll forewarn you this is not within the chain of command, but this comments on the events at the time. P01163, January 16th, 1993. This is a BritBat report, and on page 3 of the English, the last full paragraph, it says: "The HVO ops zone commander read the following message," and this is from the HVO commander, the general in Mostar: "At the Geneva Conference it was agreed that all provinces would be administrated by the leading ethnic group, in this area the Croats. The HVO and Croats fully attend to abide by this agreement. The HVO formally requests that all BiH units return to their normal locations and that all BiH units from Jajce are removed from the area. "In return, the Croats and HVO guarantee nothing will happen to the Muslim population, lest those suspected of or accused of war crimes. The Muslim population will be given full equality, but the BiH must be subordinate to the HVO. All troops must leave and fill in their trenches and all barricades are to be dismantled. Adzic, Topic, and the police command are to be removed from command. The replacements may be picked by 3rd Corps BiH Zenica, and all CPs are to be mixed, as are all police patrols. GV is to be demilitarised, and no one is to carry weapons in the town. The Bosnian media is to report the following in its bulletin: A list of demands that it should be reported that the HVO shelled no one, shot no one, and did not burn any houses, and that all these actions were carried out by the Muslims. With the media effect, the land border with Croatia is closed. There are two HVO brigades in Prozor, supported by tanks and artillery, ready to advance on Gornji Vakuf. You have until tomorrow to agree to all the demands and put them into action or face the consequences. You are to send your reply via the UNPROFOR." And then there's a comment. It says: "This is not from the HVO commander," this, I think, looks like a separate comment: "The BiH have stated that they cannot agree to all the demands. The HVO do not appear to be willing to negotiate their demands, and therefore an escalation of the conflict seems inevitable." Sir, my first question in regard to these orders that we just looked at regards the actual events at the time. Before I started this, you said you were familiar with the Vance-Owen Peace Plan; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: And were you familiar -- did you know of these orders, this -- these demands by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was familiar with the general request in that sense, i.e., that the BiH Army unit, in the territory of the HVO, to be re-subordinated, but I'm not familiar with the document, and the territory I'm talking about as belonging to the HVO was pursuant to the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So now that you've seen these documents and you see -- assuming them to be true, that the HVO demanded that certain provinces be subordinated to HVO command and that other -- other HVO units and other provinces would be subordinated to the BH -- ABiH command, assuming, in fact, that the ABiH did not do that, as you saw from other documents, they refused to subordinate their own units to the BH [sic] command, and that subsequent to their refusal, subsequent to the expiration of the dead-line, that the escalation of the conflict did, in fact, increase, would you agree with me, then, that as it regards chain of command, the lower levels of the HVO, when the escalation of the conflict increased, were aware of the orders from the top, they were aware of this chain of command and this ultimatum that was issued by first Prlic, then Stojic, then Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I have to object to the question. The facts are not in evidence. First of all, the document, signed by Dr. Prlic, is not an ultimatum, but, rather, a decision. Secondly, after three and a half years, the Prosecutor needs to know that this decision was not made by Prlic, but rather the Executive Board of the HZ-HB, and I believe it is high time for the facts to be represented the way they are in the OTP questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your objection has been recorded. Madam Prosecutor, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, as I said, again, I want you to assume these facts to be true. Would you agree with me that these orders that I just showed you, and the subsequent events resulting from the BH's refusal to agree to the HVO demands, resulting in an escalation of the conflict, in fact, is a good example of HVO efficient chain of command?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that this was a functioning chain of command. Issuing an order and sending it down to the lowest individual is one thing, and implementing such an order is an entirely different thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. We have a mistake in the transcript which is very important. Now it has been corrected. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just for the transcript, I would like to say that my learned friend from the Prosecution did not lay any grounds to claim that Mr. Stojic was part of the chain of command. Therefore, I let the witness answer. I did not want to influence his answer. That would be my objection. And my second intervention is a request. I would kindly ask my learned friend, when she moves from one binder to another, could she please indicate the location of the document. We have a problem with the five binders, and we cannot rely on the e-court only. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I would like to put a question to you. Madam Prosecutor has started reviewing all the documents from the 15th of January. My question was prompted by the response by Arif Pasalic, who was the commander of the 4th Corps of the BiH Army, and the HVO, that was later sent on the 18th of January, 1993. The document number is -- and when I read the document, I can see that Mr. Pasalic does not object to the letters that were sent saying that the units of the BiH Army in the zones 3, 8, and 10 have to be subordinated to the HVO, but he raises a big problem in paragraph 6, which seems to have escaped the attention of the diplomats and the representatives of the military and the international community in Geneva. General Pasalic says that there is a problem which concerns the soldiers who live in these areas in the south of Mostar because those people did not want to leave those territories, the regions 3, 8, and 10, and that those people didn't -- if they were not integrated into the HVO, they would be considered paramilitaries, and General Pasalic says that that shouldn't happen. Now we are in a situation which was present in mid-January, that everybody was in agreement that there should be an integrated command, but nobody took into account the specific nature of the soldiers. You say, yourself, that most brigades were territorial brigades. You are a military expert. Could you please tell us, how could all this evolve with soldiers or non-soldiers who were territorially affiliated, who wanted to stay in their own communities and municipalities, and who certainly didn't have the desire to be moved or to place themselves under the command of somebody that they were not used to or, in this case, the commanders or the command of the municipalities? Were you aware of this problem or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. All these units, the HVO and ABiH units, in the area of Northern Herzegovina were municipal units exclusively, and they were linked to a narrow stretch of territory, to their villages, and that's how they conducted warfare. When they were in the battle-field or when they went away on leave, they went home on leave, so it's quite logical to draw the conclusion Arif Pasalic drew, according to which some soldiers weren't willing. But as far as I have understood the HVO orders, they had the possibility that those Muslim units could be subordinated to the HVO. This means that they would become part of the HVO, but they could maintain their national characteristics, and that was subsequently the case. However, if they were not willing to subordinate to the HVO as Muslim units, then they were ordered to leave that area. So there were two possibilities they could opt for. I, personally, don't see why this should give rise to difficulties of any kind, especially in that that agreement or system was in place right up until May 1993, when large-scale conflicts, in fact, broke out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. A minute ago we saw two documents from Mr. Petkovic, dated the 15th of January. I had a look at the numbers carefully. They are successive numbers. When we have a look at these documents, one has the impression that General Petkovic made two types of statement. In the first document, he said it's necessary to put into place -- to implement what was decided in Geneva. All units must be subordinated either to the HVO or to the ABiH. So in his opinion, he's implementing the decisions taken in Geneva. But on the very same day, he has another document in which he's requesting that his units conduct military operations against the ABiH, and I fail to understand this change of position in this case. How would you explain it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, with regard to the second order, it's not an order to conduct combat operations. It's an order to raise the level of combat readiness. No operations are being ordered. It is only a matter of combat readiness. I think it is important to bear this in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How do you explain the fact that there are two documents, one of which encourages a return to peace, in a certain sense, and the other one is trying to prepare everyone for combat? For example, item 4 document of the 15th of January, it says: Position the artillery and two or three tanks for intervention in Vakuf and Prozor. This might seem a little perplexing. How would you analyse this, General? The document is number 66/93.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't think there is anything unusual about this. If ABiH units are prevented from leaving the territory under the control of the HVO, according to the Vance-Owen Plan, well, at the same time one can expect that in areas where conflict had broken out previously at the end of October of 1992 in Prozor or Gornji Vakuf, at key points, it is reasonable to expect that one would raise the combat -- the level of combat readiness for HVO units, because one could expect the ABiH in that area won't accept the HVO request, they won't subordinate themselves to the HVO and they won't leave that territory. As a result, an armed conflict could break out, so it's quite logical that an order was issued to raise the HVO units' level of combat readiness. That does not mean, as far as I can see from the document, that an order was issued for military operations of any kind against the ABiH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Prlic. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: I didn't want to intervene after your question, Mr. President, but it is obvious, and you mentioned that, that a number of this document is 01/66, and this so-called subordination order has a number 01/70. It is obvious that this order was issued later on, so this one doesn't -- didn't take place before this one relating to increasing of combat readiness. So from my point, if it is obvious that there is a -- Prosecutor use that in different -- in different order, which may create a different opinion about it. This is just my remark.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Ms. West. Yes. I, in fact, saw that the order on tension rising was number 66 and the order to implement the Geneva agreements was number 70, so the second document comes later, it's true, and the Prosecution proceeded in the reverse order. But all those who have seen the documents understood the fact. General, the explanation you provide us with for those two orders is that, in your opinion, the HVO thought that the ABiH would not agree to the terms and that there was going to be a conflict. That's what you're saying? Would that summarise what you have said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, one comment from the Prosecution. I don't think the comments of Mr. Prlic or Ms. Alaburic are pivotal in any way to the issues here, but my comment regards the procedure. Both of them have made factual statements, and although they may have been in response to your questions, with the hope of moving this along, under the common law process this is not something that should be considered evidence by the Trial Chamber. The only person in this room that gives evidence is the person who's in the witness stand. Even my questions are not evidence. And the Trial Chamber should be certain to only consider the statements coming from here [indicates] in its estimation. When we constantly hear comments coming from the other side, it slows down the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to move on to the issue of logistics, and I believe this is list 3 -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, perhaps there is an interpretation error. Perhaps I've understood something incorrectly, or if I've understood this correctly, in that case I don't agree with you. You're saying that the questions that you put are not part of the evidence, but when the witness answers a question, when the Judges deliberate, they'll have a look at the transcript, they'll have a look at the witness's answers, and they will also have a look at the question, because the answer is provided in response to the question. We have to take into consideration your question as well. The response is a reaction to the question. And you're saying, No, you just have to take into consideration the answer, but perhaps I have misunderstood you, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Perhaps I was not very articulate in the way I said that. Of course, if I ask a question and his answer is, Yes, then you have to understand what my question was and to understand what -- the evidence that he gives, but any question asked in this courtroom is not affirmative until evidence until you hear the answer. So when attorneys make comments in here, when the accused make comments in here, this is not evidence for your consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to the next documents, which I believe are in the binder that says "List 3" on the side, and it says "Binder 1 of 2."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, this paragraph 28 of your report. This is about a logistical support, and in your report you wrote: "Logistical support in a wartime army which is formed without peacetime preparations is significantly different. In the initial period, replenishment with combat supplies, ammunition, weapons, spare parts, is organised from equipment and reserves captured from the enemy, improvised production in secret workshops, and secret procurement from abroad." You go on to write: "With the creation of free territories and captured enemy manufacturing facilities, regular production and organised distribution is organised. With political recognition, channels for logistical support from third countries are created. Such a wartime army mostly obtains food and other quarter-master necessities from local sources. Military/territorial commands have a significant role in this." Sir, my question is: Are you of the opinion that the HVO suffered from logistical difficulties?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, I have to emphasise the fact that I wasn't involved in the details of the HVO organisation, but as far as I know, I believe that at the beginning the HVO had significant logistical problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: And when you say "at the beginning," specifically, can I have the time-frame, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be from 1992 up until the autumn of 1993. One should bear in mind the blockade in Central Bosnia, when supplies could only come in via helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: And have you seen any documents in support of this notion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have access to such documents, nor did I request that the Defence provide them. I know about this from the media and from other recordings from other sources that I followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: I'm going to show you some documents. I'm going to ask that you assume them to be true, and then we'll talk about them. The first is P00506. It should be in the binder in front of you, P00506, and it's on the screen now. This is a document dated September 19th, 1992. It's signed from -- by Tihomir Blaskic, and it says, number 1: "On checking the records, the check-point commander may give his approval for unobstructed transportation of weapons, ammunition, and military equipment, provided ..." Under A: "The weapons, ammunition, and military equipment being transported from the Republic of Croatia and the western part of the HZ-HB to Central Bosnia ...," and then it lists the zones, "are accompanied by a seal ..." And it goes on. My question is focused on the first part of this. Would you agree with me, if this document is -- we assume that it's true, that this suggests that weapons, ammunition, and military equipment is being transported from Croatia to Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: So that's September of 1992. Let's move on to February of 1993. This is P01506, P01506. It should be in the same binder. This is from February 17th, 1993, signed by Slobodan Praljak. It says a "Request for unobstructed transportation of MTS ...," and then it says: "In agreement with the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, the transport of MTS has been approved for the units of HVO in Gornji Vakuf. There are 50 MRUDs," which are mines, "in the shipment." Would you agree with me, sir, that if this is true this would suggest that the Ministry of Defence in Croatia was in agreement with the HVO to transport MTS?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: We'll move to P02510, P02510. This is May 25th, 1993, so we're going ahead a couple months. This is a security report, and it's talking about, in the very beginning --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I apologise to my learned friend. With regard to the previous document, we have the translation, and the translation, signed by Mr. Praljak, says that it is a contract, and the translation is "agreement." But in the original document, it says that an agreement is at stake. There's a big difference between an agreement and a contract. There's a significant legal difference between these two terms. Could the witness read out P011506 [as interpreted]? I apologise, the number is incorrect. P01506. This is the document we have just had a look at, the one that my colleague showed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, one should understand your comment as a comment relating to a translation error?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, yes. According to the translation, it's a contract, but the original says "agreement." The term used is "agreement."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in the text, in the document, is the term used "agreement" or "contract"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see the document on the screen right now, Your Honour, but I do remember that the term used was "agreement." If you show the document to me again, I can read it out, if you show the document to me again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we have P1000 -- the previous document, P1506, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the document on the screen, a request for unobstructed transportation of materiel and technical equipment: "In agreement with the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, the transport of MTS has been approved for the units of HVO in Gornji Vakuf." It says "in agreement."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do apologise. In Croatian, there's a difference between a contract and an agreement. The term used in the translation is "agreement" in the English. Is anyone saying something? It's translated as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That you are repeating yourself, Ms. Nozica. You had said that before, that there was a difference between "agreement" and "contract," and that is -- I think we are losing time, I'm sorry. We have now the correct word, and I do not see the relevance of this at all, I'm sorry to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that it is very relevant because there wasn't a contract, and when the witness reads this out, again we hear the word "agreement." That's why I intervened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Prosecutor, please continue with the other document.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And just for the record, on page 59, line 4, I mistakenly said "P00156." I should have said "P1506." But I will continue on to the document P02510. I believe we had it up on e-court. It's P02510, so it's the next document coming. In this, we will go forward in time. The last document we looked at was dated February of 1993, and this new document, this one in front of you now, is dated May of 1993. It's a security report. At the very beginning, it talks about the security situation in the area of responsibility of the 4th Brigade, which is not what we're looking at. But if you go down a little bit further, it finally says: "We receive frequent visits from HV Southern Front who supply equipment and provide us with advice."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, would you agree with me at least in May of 1993, this sentence would suggest that Croatia is frequently supplying equipment and advice to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see that this was frequent, but that that was the case is true. In a Sefer Halilovic order, it is stated that in co-operation with the HVO Army, they should operate in Southern Herzegovina, so I personally don't see any problems with regard to the co-operation. But as to the frequency, I can't say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: And perhaps that's a translation problem/issue. The English, as I read it, mentioned the word "frequency." Do you not see that in the Croatian?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me, may I interrupt both of you. Mr. Gorjanc has said previously that it is stated that in co-operation with the HVO Army, they should operate in Southern Herzegovina. I would like to ask you, Mr. Gorjanc, if, when you mentioned "they," then you meant HV, that is, the Croatian Army, because then it would be clear for us -- for me that they -- that even Halilovic agreed that there should be a co-operation between the HVO and the HV armies? It is my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was shown a document a few days ago, and to the extent that I have understood it, Halilovic thought that the ABiH, the Muslim side, would be cooperating, would take joint combat action with the Croatian Army in the southern battle-field, and that also means that the HVO participated in that, because the ABiH and the HVO were allies at the time. In other words, they were fighting against the Serbian aggression together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, when you said "they," it referred to ABiH army and not to HV army, not to the Croatian Army; isn't it so? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: And just to finish up on this document, to clarify, we're back to P02510, I'm looking at the English sentence which reads - this is about the fourth or fifth sentence down -: "We receive frequent visits from HV Southern Front, who supply equipment and provide us with advice." Mr. Gorjanc, do you understand that to mean that the HV, Croatia, supplied equipment and advice frequently?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it says "quite often." That's not quite as frequent as when you use the term "frequently," to the extent that I understand Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, "quite often" is fine. We move on to P02975, P02975. We're moving ahead in time to June 27th, 1993, and this is a -- it looks like it's a receipt. It says: "The Special Purpose Unit of the GSHV gives the following materiel and technical equipment to the Mostar HVO for temporary use:" And then number 1 -- do you have this document in front of you, sir? Okay, so you see number 1. It says: "A ULM White Hopper," and then it gives a number and a motor number. Number 2 is: "Additional equipment: A parachute for the launching rocket, one GPS with a serial number, two radios, two headphones with microphones and adapters." Sir, would you agree with me that this is -- this illustrates that at least by June 27th 1993, the Croatian government was still giving material to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with these products, but obviously the Croatian government gave them to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Okay, sir, thank you. We'll move forward in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Really, Your Honours, I do apologise, but it never mentions the Croatian government here. Surely, at such a lofty international court, we should read the text as it is written. This is a private correspondence. There's no Croatian government, or army, or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your intervention has been recorded in the transcript, and I ask the English booth to press the buttons properly so I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We'll move on to P04930, P04930. This is September 10th, 1993, and this is the Republic of Croatia Command of the Southern Front letterhead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you again. I'm sorry to interrupt you, Ms. West, but I have to come back to what we have heard from Mr. Praljak. He referred to the fact that, referring to that kind of letter, that the letter never mentions the Croatian government here: "Surely --" I continue to quote him: "Surely at such a lofty international court, we should read the text as it is written. This is a private correspondence. There is no Croatian government, or army, or anything like that." Of course, it is not my role to make comments on what Mr. Praljak here stated, but, of course, this one is coming -- I mean, the letter, what we have before us, it is from the Croatian Army Main Staff, from the Croatian Army Main Staff, and it cannot be, of course, meant and cannot be qualified as a private correspondence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: P04930, which is September 10th, and this is on the letterhead of the Republic of Croatia, Command of the Southern Front, and the subject is: "Replenishing units with technical equipment and materiel." If you go to the second page in English, the substance of the letter is: "Pursuant to the request for replenishment of technical equipment," and then I think there's supposed to be a number there, "of September 10th, 1993, with a view to resupplying HVO units (Mr. Tole) with approved quantities of technical equipment and materiel, on September 10th, issued from the reserves -- the auxiliary logistics base, the depot, the following quantities of technical equipment and materiel:" And then it lists them. The first is 122-millimetre shells for a self-propelled gun, 100 pieces, and the second is for the auxiliary logistics base, the HVO vehicle has already started out and will report. At the bottom, it says: "The equipment can be issued to an authorised individual from an HVO unit." Sir, would you agree with me that this -- at least September 10th would suggest that the Republic of Croatia continues to supply the HVO with the technical equipment and materiel?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: And we'll do one more document, which is P03071, P03071. This is dated July 1, 1993. It's from Bruno Stojic and it's to -- at the top, it says "ROJS." I won't pronounce that, but assume for the facts of this question that that person is a general in the Croatian Army. It's a request for artillery ammunition: "Since we are left with no artillery ammunition for 203-millimetre Howitzers and 152-millimetre Howitzers, please deliver to us whatever quantity may be possible." Would you agree with me again, sir, that in this letter or this document, we see that Mr. Stojic is making a request from the Croatian Army for MTS?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: I'm going to read four facts to you. These are adjudicated facts, but for the purposes of my question just assume these facts to be true. The first is: Apart from providing manpower, Croatia also lent substantial material assistance to the HVO in the form of financial and logistical support. That's the Blaskic trial judgement, paragraph 120. The second fact is: The Republic of Croatia financed and provided military equipment to the HVO in the course of its conflict with the ABiH. The provision of assistance, in terms of military equipment, was considerable. The presence of large numbers of HV vehicles and weaponry was reported on many occasions. It's Tuta Stela trial judgement paragraph 199. And the third fact is Croatia supplied the HVO with large quantities of arms and materiel in 1992, 1993, 1994. It's the Blaskic trial judgement, paragraph 120. And, lastly, HVO commanders would address requests for ammunition to Susak directly. It's Tuta Stela trial judgement paragraph 199. Now, assuming all the facts -- those four facts that I just read to you are true, would you agree with me that unlike the wartime army that you write about in paragraph 28, the HVO appears to be logistically funded by the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can just have a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I take advantage of the time to ask the witness: Did you also know that the Republic of Croatia sent arms to the HVO so that a part of those arms should also go to the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is obvious from these documents, and there were reports in the media to that effect also. Your Honour, I didn't quite understand your question. Could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you know that the Republic of Croatia sent weapons and materiel to the HVO, but that a part of those weapons and materiel were intended for the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: And following up on that: Have you ever seen any documents or have you ever heard any media reports suggesting that the Republic of Croatia was sending weapons and materials to the ABiH, subsequent to March 1993, in areas within Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, for that period, no, but for the period before that, I found many documents on General Praljak's web site.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move to paragraph 88 of your report, and it's in this part of your report you talk about the composition of the armed forces. And in 88, you write: "With the decree law on amendments to the decree law on the Armed Forces of RBH of 18 July 1992, the RBH Presidency expanded the concept of armed forces of the RBH so that self-organised armed formations or those organised into illegal military units under different names as part of the forces resisting the fascist occupation of the BiH by the so-called ...," and then you talk about who was attacking. In regard to this particular part of your report, sir, you cite document 1D01230, and we don't have to look at that at this moment, and you indicate that it was dated 18 July of 1992. Just so I understand, in paragraph 88 you suggested that in July of 1992, the BiH Presidency was expanding its notion of armed forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: And then the following paragraph, you write that: "In August of 1992," now this is just a month later, "the BH Presidency again changed the definition of the concept of armed forces in the decree law on the armed forces, so from that moment on, the armed forces consisted of the army of the republic, and its components were HVO units and other armed groups, which put themselves under the unified command of the army." So here is it your position that in the summer of 1992, the Bosnian-Herzegovinian Presidency was of the practice of expanding its notion of its armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So you indicate that this happened twice in the summer of 1992. The first is July 18th, 1992, and for you that's -- you cite it in your footnote, and you cite 1D01240, which will be in the second binder. It says "List 3" on the side, and it's the second binder, but you're going to see it in front of you in a moment. That's 1D01240. And, sir, I just really want to focus on the date of this document, because it seems -- from the English, I'll read the date on the second page. It says "18 July 1993." And I believe the B/C/S also says "18 July 1993." Can you see that in front of you? Maybe you can go to the second page of the B/C/S and tell me the date.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 18th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So in your report, in paragraph 88, you indicate that it was 1992. Is that just -- I assume that that's just a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: The reason I focused on that is because in paragraph 89, you wrote: "In August 1992, the BH Presidency again changed its definition ." So, in fact, it shouldn't be "again" in this case, it just should be "changed its definition"; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that if I have been following properly, confusion may arise. In the text written by Mr. Gorjanc, in the Croatian version we don't find the year 1993 anywhere, and the document we have on the screen just now is one document, and a second document are the changes in August 1992, which is document 4D410. And if we show the witness the report and these documents -- unless we do that, I think it is difficult, even for a lawyer, to respond, not to mention a military man.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I think I can do that fairly quickly, just to simplify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, if you're looking at the screen in front of you, this is the document upon which you based your paragraph 88. Now, just to be quick about this, I'm going to hand you your paragraph 88. Now, the document in front of you is dated July of 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: But when you wrote it in paragraph 88, you actually wrote "July of 1992"; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: And so in paragraph 89, when you wrote that the BH Presidency expanded again its notion of armed forces, in fact, this is not "again," this is -- from your perspective, it would be the first time, in the summer of 1992, that they expanded their notion; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: So let's focus on your paragraph 89. In that paragraph, you cite document 4D00410, and I believe that's going to be in binder 2 of list 3. It's 4D00410, and this is the paragraph where you wrote: "In August of 1992, the BH Presidency," and we'll get rid of the word "again," "the RBH Presidency changed the definition of the concept of armed forces in the decree law on the armed forces so that from that moment on the armed forces consisted of the army of the republic, and its components were HVO units and other armed groups which put themselves under the unified command of the army." You then wrote: "During a state of war, in addition to the army, the armed forces consist of the police, physical security units, of companies, and other legal entities, customs/service units, and other border organs who re-subordinate themselves under the unified command of the armed forces." And that's when you cite this document, so let's focus on this document. Looking at Article 1, second paragraph: "The republic's armed forces shall comprise the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina (hereinafter the army), a constituent part of the army shall comprise the Croatian Defence Council, as well as other armed compositions which place themselves under the single command of the army." Mr. Gorjanc, when you were writing paragraph 89 in your report, at least the first part of it, it was to this part of the article that you were referring; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to look at P00339.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you move on to the next document, the document that we have in front of us, which is signed by Mr. Izetbegovic, it is dated August 1992 and it says, in Article 1, that the HVO is a component part of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you agree with that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is what is written here, Your Honour, but in fact -- in fact, it was different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why was it different, in fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of my knowledge, the HVO was independent in relation to the army. It was an independent, autonomous partner which only acted together with it or cooperated once the conflict ceased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Madam West.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, we're going to look at P00339. It's the first binder, excuse me. Mr. Gorjanc, it's the first binder of these two, but you should see it on the screen shortly, P00339. This is the agreement on friendship and co-operation between the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia, and it is this agreement which was the impetus for the constitutional amendment that you cite, 4D004110 [sic]. Have you seen this agreement before?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: So you'll be familiar with number 6 of the agreement, paragraph 6? It says: "The armed component of the Croatian Defence Council is an integral part of the united armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." So let's just focus on that very first sentence. Would you agree with me that that language would suggest that the armed forces of the Republic BiH, as you described, consisted of the HVO, and you also wrote some other groups?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the previous document, we saw that the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina consist of the Army of the BH, HVO, and other armed units that placed themselves under a unified command. Here, it says that the armed component of the Croatian Defence Council is a component part of the unified armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia, which means that it is on an equal footing with the army and it has the same status.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, let's go into -- let's look at that a little bit closer. We're still on P00339, number 6, and I want to focus solely on this language, because you know, as I'm sure you do, the amendment came after the fact. So let's focus on the July 21 language. It says: "The armed component of the Croatian Defence Council is an integral part of the united armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Stop. Where in there tells us that the HVO is on equal footing with the ABiH and it has the same status? Where do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this wording, no, but -- in this wording, you don't find that, but bearing in mind the document that came later, one can conclude that when the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina established that the armed forces consist of the army, the HVO, and other units, then from this I conclude that the HVO was an equal partner to the Army of ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. First let's go back to what you based your report on, which is 4D00410, and I suspect it will be on the screen in a moment. As you said, you don't find the wording there, but bearing in the document that came later, and I think you're talking about this amendment, that's where you suggest you find the word "equality," so let's have a look at that. And Article 1 says: "The republic's armed forces shall comprise the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. A constituent part of the army shall comprise the Croatian Defence Council as well as other armed compositions which place themselves under the single command of the army." So, sir, doesn't that mean that the HVO and the other armed compositions, "place --" and I'll quote here, "place themselves under the single command of the" ABiH army? Isn't that what that means?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says, but I'm not an expert on constitutional law and my personal opinion is that this was speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But your answer earlier is that in regard to this document, one can conclude that when the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina established that the armed forces consists of the army, the HVO, and other units, then from this, so this document we're talking about, "I conclude that the HVO was an equal partner to the Army of the BiH." Sir, do you see the word "equal" in here? How do you come to that conclusion, based on this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say that. But bearing in mind the actual state of affairs in Bosnia at the time, I assumed they were equal partners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I must apologise. I didn't want to interrupt you. Please finish your sentence, and then I have a small question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, Your Honour. I lost the thread of my thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It could happen to me as well. I was going to ask you about a part of this definition which we have not yet approached, but -- I'm sorry, Ms. West, if I'm doing what you were about to do. This does not simply say the HVO armed component is part of the ABiH, but it is limited to the armed compositions of the HVO which place themselves under the single command of the army. Does that refer, in your view, to the HVO Army or to the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the reference here is made to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm surprised, because the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the first sentence, is followed by "(hereinafter the army)." Would that not indicate that when later on, without qualifications, the words "the army" come up, that it refers to the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Now the question arises: Can you tell the Chamber which, if any, components of the HVO have, in fact, at the moment of this document, 15 November 1992, placed themselves under the single command of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, and I believe that at that moment there was no single HVO unit that would have been directly under the command of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Excuse me for the interruption, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we're talking about legal matters which may be beyond your knowledge.
