However, if you are familiar with the document and its paragraph 6, there are two things which seem, as my colleague has just said, that the HVO was not an element either of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- there was an integrated army, that's evident, but within that army, and it's written black on white, that the HVO had its representatives in the joint command, the armed forces, which means that the HVO participates in the joint command of the two militaries. What does that mean for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This would have been a command that would have been composed of both Muslims and Croats. Its headquarters would have been in Sarajevo, and at the lower levels the commands should also have been composed of the representatives of both armed structures in Bosnia-Herzegovina, at least at the operational level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is already time for a break. We're going to take 20 minutes, and then we will come back at 5 past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, you wanted to have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you, Your Honour. [In English] The Praljak Defence respectfully requests leave to reply to all responses to our Rule 92 bis motion which we filed on 14 September, and we also ask to permit us to file this reply on or before 30 November. To remind you, the Trial Chamber granted an extension for all parties who wished to respond to our 92 bis motion, permitting them over six weeks to respond. A total of five parties took advantage of that extension, and one party took advantage of responding twice. We received those responses starting from 26 and last one on 29 October. The responses are, to say the least, extensive. I will not elaborate further. We made no objection to the request for the extension of time for other parties to respond, since we recognised the need for a full and fair airing of views. The Trial Chamber invited the Praljak Defence to file a reply subsequent to 28th October, following our request to reply on 23rd September, since the Prosecution at that time filed provisional response. In that request, we have listed in detail 11 reasons a reply was required, all of which remain valid. In addition, now there are also other parties responding, and we also have a lot of reasons to reply. So those 11 points are precisely listed in our earlier motion -- in our earlier submission filed on 23rd September. I don't think that I have to read them now. We all can check that easily. With the additional responses filed by the other parties, there is additional material requiring a reply. The material in the responses is wide ranging, it's going from a particular issue, regarding a particular document or statement, to broad legal issues. We believe the Trial Chamber would best be served by having a full and considerate reply to certain items in the various responses. That is my submission, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Douglas Stringer appearing for the Prosecution. I know that the application that's just been made is directed to reply not only to the Prosecution response but to the responses filed by other Defence teams as well, and so obviously the Prosecution response would only apply to our own submission on that. And in respect of a reply, we don't have a position. I think that it's for the Trial Chamber to decide whether it believes that a reply is needed or not, and so we don't have a position on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will confer with my colleagues now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber, having deliberated, having conferred, grants the Praljak Defence team the possibility of replying to these responses by the 30th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, you described the definition of "siege" as it related to East Mostar in your report, beginning at paragraph 2001 [sic] to 214, and your conclusion in paragraph 214 is that East Mostar was not under siege; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: And in paragraph 203, you write about a modern military siege, according to the principle of US military, and then you go on to define it. What is the source of your definition?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A rule that applies to this definition is the field manual for the American military called "Operations," and I quote -- I believe that I have quoted that in English. I must say that the JNA did not have any special provisions and categories for a siege or an encirclement around a town. Towns, as such, were subject of combat activities in case of war. However, we liberated our own towns, and in compliance with the doctrine of All-People's Defence this was done from the inside, and that's why we did not have the classical interpretation of "siege" and we did not elaborate that notion at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: So if we can back up, you said that a rule that applies to this definition is the field manual for the American military. Now, you don't cite that field manual in your report, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I did. I quoted it. Because I did not have it in the original, in a hard copy, I downloaded that from a web page which contains all American military field manuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And it may be that you're referring to footnote 147, where you say a siege is to surround a city or enemy army, cutting off supplies, in order to force surrender; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I cannot see the footnote, itself. Could the page be scrolled up a little to display the foot page -- the footnote? No, this is only an interpretation in English to show what that implies according to that military rule. If I remember the whole thing well, I hope that this is the FM-3 manual under the title "Operations."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So I've looked through your report on this part, and I don't see any reference to the US manual, but are you telling us that footnote 147 is to the US manual, field manual?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Your Honours, I can bring that tomorrow. I have it on my laptop. And I can tell you tomorrow what manual I was quoting from.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: That's not necessary. I just needed to understand where you got it from, and now I do understand. But the next paragraph is paragraph 2005 [sic], in which you write -- excuse me, 205, and you write that: "The basic principle of a siege or blockade is complete isolation." And then you go on to say that in modern military theory, this can be physical, electronic, psychological. Is this also -- does this also come from the American field manual?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was completely taken over from the American Army field manual.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: All right. So let's separate this out, and the first one we want to talk about is physical isolation. And you testified last week, in regard to a question from Judge Antonetti -- he asked: "All right. In this light, would you agree, as a military expert, with the fact that one can say that Mostar is a city under siege, like Sarajevo, or that Mostar is in a different kind of situation?" And your answer was that: "Mostar was in a substantially different situation." He then asked: "How different?" And your answer was: "To the north, where the main reserves of the BH Army were, there were two roads leading. One was down the Neretva River Valley, which was most probably under fire, under artillery fire, HVO artillery fire, and the other route took one across a mountainous area, the western slopes of Mount Prenj and on towards Jablanica. That route was not under fire by the HVO." So that we understand, is it your testimony that when we focus on the physical, that to the north there were two roads, one along the valley that's close to the HVO line and then one over the mountain to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both are northbound, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: All right. So I think the answer to that is, Yes. And let's first talk about the road to the north that's on the Neretva Valley road that you said was under artillery fire. Now, the reason, Mr. Gorjanc, that it was under HVO fire was that it was so close to the HVO front-line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so. I didn't see any documents, but there was a plateau -- an area around the Vrdi village under the control of the HVO. It's two or three kilometres from that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: And you'll agree with me that if one chose to travel along that road, one would be subject to the artillery fire of the HVO; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: And that was both risky and dangerous; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: All right. So if we look at 4D00622, this is the map that you made, which I think will come up. Is that correct, this is the map you made? This is list 2 -- the binder that indicates "List 2" on the spine. If you look at this map and if we focus in on where the blue meets the green, you'll agree with me that's the -- that's where the HVO front-line comes close to meeting the ABiH front-line; correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, if I may just intervene briefly. If I've understood the question correctly, the suggestion is being made that the witness compiled this map that is on the screen, drafted the map. If that's what is being suggested, I'd like to say it's not correct. This document has been an exhibit for a long time now, and the General Petkovic Defence, in fact, provided this document, drafted this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Alaburic. That is my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: But you've seen this document before; correct? This is one that was shown to you by the Petkovic Defence? So if you -- for the purposes of your testimony in this case, we're going to assume that the Petkovic Defence line, where the HVO comes close to meeting the ABiH, is the front-line after June 30th, 1993. So now I'm going to show you P11081. This is another map, and the reason I'm showing you this map is because it's a far more detailed map, and I think it will be more workable. And I'm only -- this is a map that was drawn by the BH government after -- after August of 1993, and I am only interested to know, if you will look and tell me, whether the front-line drawn on the Petkovic Defence map and the front-line on this BH government map is about the same. And I'm actually going to hand it to you. So I'm not interested in any of the writing on it. I'm not suggesting to you that that's factual or not. My question is: Would you agree with me that it appears that at least the front-lines coincide?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: So let's work off the more detailed map I showed you, which is P11081, and we're going to enlarge it on the screen for you, and I'll give you a copy as well just so you can make sure -- we can make sure that you see it. Now, for the purposes of these questions, the blue line is the ABiH front-line, and the red line is the HVO front-line. Now, do you see the city of Mostar sort of in the middle?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: And you see leading out of Mostar north, we have one road that's going north right through East Mostar, another road that's going north that's kind of behind East Mostar, but they hook up as we get close to Rastani? Would you agree with me this road going north, the one in down-town East Mostar, is the main road that you've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: So if you look at the distance from that main road going through East Mostar to the red line, would you agree with me, if we look at some of the other distances on this map, so, for example, as we get up in the area near Rastani, we see between the red and the blue is 250 metres, would you agree with me that from down-town Mostar -- from that road to the red line is somewhere a little bit more than 250 metres or probably not more than 400 metres?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the center of Mostar to that line, do you mean from the Croatian lines to the armija lines, to the ABiH lines?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, if you go right to the center of Mostar, and you'll see right down --

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Right down, and you go west, the distance from that road going west to that red line, looking at the rest of this map and seeing how distances are measured, about how far is that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in some cases even less, but the road goes through settlements at these places and it's protected by buildings, and this area can only be fired on by mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Very good. But in your direct testimony, you conceded that this road was subject to HVO artillery fire; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that the upper part that you can't see in the map, in the Dreznica area -- well, the Dreznica area was under HVO artillery fire, and in the town, given the contact between the forces, there was a very small distance, well naturally this was possible, it was possible to open fire there. And the ABiH also returned fire in the direction of Croatian territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Right. What we're focused on now is the main road and how close it is to the HVO main line. I want you to go north a bit, and if you continue to go north the road kind of turns to the right, and it goes under the area of Rastani, and this is the area, for the purposes of my question, I want you to assume that in this area, after August of -- August 24th, 1993, the HVO took over that area. So the area that you see that has diagonal slash lines, consider that to be HVO territory. Would you agree with me that that road comes within 50 metres of the Rastani occupied HVO territory at one point?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, there isn't universal following of this map and everywhere we're going on it. I'm not the only one -- we're not finding this easy. Somebody needs to use some sort of pointer so that we can see specifically what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Ms. West, Mr. Stewart is quite right. I'm finding it difficult to follow you. To be quite frank, I'm somewhat lost. It would be best to use a pointer. You could use the ELMO, you could make your presentation in that way, because right now it is a little difficult to understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. I appreciate that, Your Honour. Maybe if I put it on the ELMO, then the witness could mark it and you could all following along.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the meantime if we could know who drew this map and which period is concerned in relation to this map so that we know what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. At the beginning, I mentioned that this was a BH government map and it reflects the area subsequent to June - thank you - 24th, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may, the information is not really useful. The Croatian government is rather extensive -- BH government, sorry, and we would like to have more precise information; not only the agency of the government, which one it is, but also the person, because that would be interesting to challenge the evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, at the beginning of my questions to the witness regarded the first map, because I understand the comments being made by the Defence, and as I mentioned early on, my purposes for this map was only to use it because it's more detailed in terms of roads, and that's why I compared this map to 4D0422, which is a Petkovic map, to show that the front-lines are quite similar. I don't -- I don't know -- you know, we cannot use the Petkovic map because it is not detailed. The witness has indicated that this map is quite similar when it comes to the front-lines, so it's unclear to me why we can't use a more detailed map. Now, in terms of admissibility, I certainly can hear the objections for that, but for right now, for the purposes of my questions, I think this map is completely appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this information is maybe useful, but it is not what we require. I think that the precise source of the map should be disclosed, because otherwise we cannot argue about the validity of that, especially because this is not yet in evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think two observations fall to be made. First, the map is actually signed. The name -- are you interested in what I'm saying, Mr. Kovacic? The name of the author, prefaced with the word "author," is to be found on the bottom right-hand corner. It is handwritten. I confess that I am not able to read it, but someone might be. And, second, I would suggest as the Defence have a map, that they prepare themselves. The Prosecution pretends that there are no differences. Whenever a question is put and something is raised which the Defence does disagree and thinks it is not the same as on the Petkovic map, then that be could brought into the open. I understand that it's not even the intention to file this map as a piece of evidence, but it's just being used as being technically superior, as the Prosecution says, than the Petkovic map, and I would think that as the Defence -- all Defences have the possibility to point to differences, that should then -- should then do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look, we want Madam West to make a presentation. Madam West, take the pointer and show us where the road is, in your opinion, and then put the question. Everything else is of secondary importance. We have the good fortune to have a road.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: So, Mr. Gorjanc, looking at this map, and I'm going to point, here [indicates] is East Mostar, or -- can you see on the map where East Mostar is, you know, the down-town area of East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: From that down-town area, going west to that red line, assuming these other --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can I make an observation, Your Honour? This is all going to have to be comprehensible on the transcript, so that it's difficult -- I know it's a difficult task, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No, it's not difficult, Mr. Stewart. What I'll have the witness do is mark it when I'm done asking the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, sorry. It was actually kind of a comment made supportive of you --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And I appreciate --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- [Overlapping speakers] sometimes it's difficult, actually, making such a thing clear. If you find it incredibly easy, then congratulations.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: So if you go from down-town East Mostar going west to that red line, and using, say, that -- that the estimate is 750 metres, that's 250 metres [indicates], that's 750 metres [indicates], using those as a guide, can you estimate for me how far it is from this road line to the red HVO front-line?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's at the exit from Mostar towards the north. It's in the area of the train station. It's about 200 metres to the Neretva River.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: I'm going to have you draw on this map that line, and you can indicate that it's 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, let the witness testify. He is testifying. He has just marked the distance of 200 metres. Madam, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: And if right next to that line you just drew, if you can write "200 metres."

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So now, if we go from, let's say, about this right here [indicates] to the red line, can you make a line and write in about how many metres you think that is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that the distance would be 750 metres [marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And earlier I mentioned that I want you to assume for me that after the 24th -- excuse me, August 24th, 1993, that the area of Rastani was taken over -- taken back by the HVO. For the record -- yeah, exactly. I want you to make a mark -- THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: -- from the continuation of that road to the area of Rastani and give me an estimation on how far you think that is.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, what is it that you would like to say? I am following the witness quite clearly. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for technical reasons relating to this map, I'd like to say the following: The scale is 1:1.000.000 [as interpreted]. Ask the witness, a centimetre on the map, how much does that relate to real life, if the scale is 1:1.000.000 [as interpreted]. One centimetre cannot represent 200 metres here. You know, that's the problem. The scale of the map, it says "1:100.000." So what does 1 centimetre represent, and then we can see what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It represents 1 kilometre. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Then we have to measure 1 centimetre so that it represents a kilometre. It would not be 250 metres in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, if what Mr. Petkovic says is true, he says that the scale of the map is 1:100.000, and therefore 1 centimetre would represent 1 kilometre. You are a general, just like he is, or you're a colonel or a general, so you should be in agreement when it comes to military maps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The scale of the map is 1:100.000 and that means that 1 centimetre on the map represents 1 kilometre in reality, and this means that there should be -- one square should represent 2 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you say that 1 centimetre is a metre, then there are mistakes that one can notice immediately on the map. When I see "1.7 kilometres," well, in this case we have more than 2 centimetres, and when I say "4.7 kilometres," well, on the map we have more than 4 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have to look at the coordination network on the map, because this map has been reduced in size and this one enlarged, so the representation is erroneous. We have a square, 2 kilometres by 2 on a map, the scale of which is 1:100.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you say one square, it's -- it represents 2 kilometres, 2, not 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 2, that's right. 1 centimetre on the map represents 1 kilometre, and the coordination network is unique, it's a single one. It means that one square is 2 kilometres by 2. It should have the size -- it should be 2 centimetres, but here it is smaller. And on the other map, it is bigger. That's why I was confused, because I could -- on the basis of the square, I thought it was the scale of 1:20.000, because on a map of 1: -- the scale of which is 1:25.000, the coordinate network is 1 by 1. The grid, the coordination grid is 1 by 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's allow Madam West to continue. She wanted to show that the road was, in fact, very close to the HVO front-lines. Ms. West, please continue, and we'll see about the distance later, and in particular with regard to Rastani.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and I'm just going to back up on the record because it appears that something wasn't recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: I had asked you, at page 94, line 18: "From the continuation of that road to the area of Rastani, can you give me an estimate on how far you think that is?" And it was at that point that you wrote in "50 to 100 metres." Did you say that out loud? Or let me ask you again. How far is that distance from Rastani to the road?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's over 200 metres here, if I take into consideration the scale of the map, because I thought the scale of the map was 1:25.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it would be useful to first locate Rastani, and then we could determine the distance between, I assume, Eastern Mostar and Rastani.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, could you point out the location of Rastani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Rastani is on the right bank of the Neretva River in the northern part of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but could you do so on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the map, it's to the north, it's this area here [indicates], it's in this area here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So the question is a key question. The road that we can see, how far is this road from the HVO lines after the HVO took control of Rastani? Is it 50 metres, 100 metres, 200 metres?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do persist with the observation I made earlier. Your Honour says -- it's not Your Honour's fault, no criticism at all, but "the road that we can see." We are going to need such things to be very clearly marked, and better -- the sooner the better as we go along, but they're going to have to be clearly marked because we can see lots of roads here. So it's -- with respect, I think this task is more difficult for counsel sometimes than is appreciated, and let's take it, at the right place, to get it clear, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, you asked for the admission of this map, since you asked the witness to indicate distance. Now that we know where Rastani is, we know that the distance is 50 to 100 metres, 50 to 100 metres. Could you please point to the route with the pointer?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, I think you can point to that road. You can even mark it with your pen, mark the road with your pen.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. That's the road, and this is Rastani [indicates]. The entire area is Rastani.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: And so the -- what would be the HVO front-line after they took over the area from Rastani to that road, is that 50 to 100 metres, like you wrote on the map?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will please forgive me. I believe that the scale of this map was bigger. However, when I take into account that this is a map whose scale is 1:100.000, then the distance is about 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Why don't you make that correction on the map. Go ahead and make that correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, what is it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I must persist with this, Your Honour, because we are going to have work from this transcript later. The witness says that's the road, and then he makes some marking, and the transcript doesn't tell us what marking he's made, so when we look at the transcript a few months down the line, we're going to have to guess what the marking is that goes with the remark he's made because he put a block around Rastani. It really is -- it needs to be -- if we're going to have to use this material later, it does need to be taken more carefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think Mr. Stewart is perfectly right. If one looks at the text in isolation, one cannot make heads or tails, so I think as we are about to close, there is perhaps some homework for tonight to think of a way how this can be presented in a way that is useful for the transcript. In technical terms, I cannot refrain from recalling that this map is 1:100.000, and the distance between the lines is, on the map, in the original, 1 kilometre. This is, I suspect, already a slightly enlarged map. That's why it looks larger than 1 centimetre. It probably is. So we have to reduce this. On the screen, of course, it's again much bigger. We have a number of indications of this map which at first glance seem to me quite plausible, and that, I think, is something which allows to make estimates, because it is a basis that perhaps someone wants to contest. I -- for the moment, I see no reasons to doubt it. And then the map, itself, with these indications, I think, can be of a certain use, subject, of course, to all corrections and criticisms the Defences want to apply to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I just have one more moment to wrap this up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, on the map on the ELMO, can you sign the bottom and put today's date, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May this have an IC number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to give it an IC number, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to provide clarification. The fact that the map has been signed, does this mean that we are done with the map or are we going to continue talking about it tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, for record purposes -- Your Honour, for the record, the marked version of the map shall be given Exhibit IC01088. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to understand the issue of the map, I am going to say this for the transcript: In addition to the reference to 200 metres made by the witness, we see that the author of the map, on the left, between the red and blue lines, marked "220 metres," and there are three arrows and you will see "220 metres." And we can conclude that if the author of the map is not mistaken, 220 metre distance can be visualised in the -- very close to the reference to 200 metres that the witness has made, and everybody can see it. Ms. West will probably come back to the issues tomorrow, but I believe that this road was close to the HVO lines, and in any case somewhere around 200 metres or less than that. In any case, we are going to continue tomorrow, in the afternoon, 2.15. Good evening to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May I have one more comment? My apologies. I think it might help this situation if the witness took the map with him overnight, and maybe he can take a look at it, and if we decide to go into it tomorrow, he will have an equal -- a valuable opportunity to take a look at it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Give him the map. He's going to study it, and he is going to bring it back tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
